title: In The Heat Of The Night

contact_edits.before: Kevin Hanchard matches her as a John with complementary hang-ups: sure of himself as a man, but still jumping shamefully to attention at the ring of the master's phone (a particularly effective update). He's cruel without being naturally callous; he has just as much compassion as he can afford. He's nettled and shamed not only by Julie but -- Strindberg's notorious misogyny being on hold in this play --by Raven Dauda's spirited and sensible Christine who, all dressed up in her Sunday-go-to-meeting, gives the play's religious imperatives an unaccustomed authority. She also, in an uncommonly handsome kitchen, attacks her chopping-block with an implacability that foreshadows the dispatching of Miss Julie's pet. Some of the scene setting is heavy-handed; John reads about Lyndon Johnson's signing of the Civil Rights Act and the murder of the freedom riders Goodman, Schwerner and Chaney in the same edition of the daily paper, dated the Fourth of July. And The Real Inspector Hound should have killed off the device by which, whenever someone turns on the radio, it's right at the start of either a song or a news bulletin. But most of the details fit beautifully into place. The brief shared dream of opening a jazz-club in Chicago--John as manager, Julie as hostess, Christine as cook-- rings true for all three of them; they must all have seen the same movies. The play Miss Julie is supposed to have the tension of an erotic nightmare. For once it does. - Miss Julie: Freedom Summer is at the Bluma Appel Theatre until March 7. For tickets and information call 416-368-3110
